title: Super-resolution Control of Two-dimensional Quantum Emitters
authors: Bosai Lyu, Valeria Vento, Ludivine Fausten, Daniel Suarez-Forero, Klevis Domi, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Alberto Morpurgo, Iaroslav Gaponenko, Patrycja Paruch, Ajit Srivastava
abstract: Localized interlayer excitons in semiconducting transition-metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers are quantum emitters with a static electric dipole moment, making them excellent nanoscale charge sensors to probe correlated quantum phases in a proximal layer. These emitters are electrically tunable and inherit spin-valley selection rules, yet their deterministic spatial control remains challenging due to subwavelength confinement. Here, we present a platform that combines cryogenic optical spectroscopy with scanning probe microscopy to investigate trapped interlayer excitons in WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ bilayers. By exploiting AFM-based local Stark shift, we achieve super-resolution localization of emitters separated by only a few tens of nanometers and demonstrate deterministic control of individual charge states, including trion formation, opening a path towards coherent inter-dot coupling. Time-resolved measurements reveal tip-induced modification of the electromagnetic vacuum around individual emitters, thus controlling their radiative emission. Our multi-point charge sensing platform with optical readout is particularly well-suited to study fractionalization and anyon dynamics in semiconducting FCIs.
summary: The researchers developed a Quantum Optical Super-resolution Microscope (QOSMic) to study interlayer excitons in TMD heterobilayers. By using an AFM tip, they achieved super-resolution spatial mapping and deterministic control over the charge state of individual emitters. This platform allows for the precise study of quantum phenomena like anyon dynamics by locally tuning the emitter's electronic and photonic environment.
main_problem: The primary goal is to achieve super-resolution spatial control and deterministic charge state control of two-dimensional quantum emitters to probe complex correlated quantum phases.
main_result: The authors demonstrated super-resolution localization of emitters separated by tens of nanometers and achieved deterministic control over individual charge states, opening pathways for studying coherent inter-dot coupling.
method: They utilized a novel Quantum Optical Super-resolution Microscope (QOSMic) combining cryogenic optical spectroscopy with an AFM tip to locally modify the electrostatic environment and photonic density of states around the emitters.
model_or_system: The system involves localized interlayer excitons in semiconducting TMD heterobilayers ($	ext{WSe}_2/	ext{MoSe}_2$) encapsulated by hBN. The control mechanism relies on the permanent dipole moment interacting with the local electric field generated by the AFM tip.
key_observables: Stark shift in PL energy, local charge state (doping) transitions (e.g., trion formation), and modification of the emission lifetime ($	au$) due to local photonic density of states (LPDOS) changes.
important_parameters: Spatial resolution down to $\sim 40 	ext{ nm}$; cryogenic temperatures ($	ext{4 K}$); applied bias voltages ($V_{	ext{tip}}, V_{	ext{bg}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the local electric field via the Stark shift ($\Delta E = -\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r})$) and assuming the tip modifies the LPDOS in a quantifiable manner.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QOSMic setup, raster scans mapping energy shifts across multiple emitters, and plots detailing the dependence of PL energy and lifetime on tip position and applied bias voltages.
paper_structure: The paper details the QOSMic setup, presents measurements showing super-resolution mapping of energy shifts and charge state control via tip scanning, and analyzes the resulting lifetime modifications linked to LPDOS changes.
why_interesting: This work provides an exquisite example of using scanning probe techniques to engineer and probe quantum emitters at the nanoscale, directly relevant to understanding open quantum systems and cavity QED effects in solid-state materials.
